title: The Kingdom of Crooked Mirrors
author: Vitaly Gubarev
short_summary: Olya, who puts everything off, always has an excuse and is rude to her grandmother, hears her grandmother wish that the girl could just once see herself from the outside. That same day the hall mirror speaks, and Olya steps through it into a kingdom where everything is reversed. There she meets her own reflection, a girl called Yalo with exactly the same faults — in a country where crooked mirrors lie to people, and a boy is sentenced to death for breaking one.
extended_summary:
Olya quarrels with her grandmother, who sighs that it would do the girl good to see herself from the outside. Left alone, Olya pulls faces at the hall mirror — and the mirror answers her. She steps through the frame and meets Yalo: her reflection, now a separate girl, with the same sulks and the same laziness.

In the kingdom they have entered, names are read backwards and mirrors show everything as it is not. The chief minister, Nushrok, owns every mirror workshop in the country; when a starving boy worker called Gurd looks into one, it shows him a fat boy holding an enormous loaf. Gurd shouts that the mirrors lie and smashes one — and for that he is chained on the roof of the Tower of Death and sentenced to be executed.

Olya and Yalo disguise themselves as pages and get inside the palace. The key to Gurd's chains hangs above the king's throne; the girls take it, lose it on the road, and go after the second key, which belongs to the minister Abazh. In the middle of a quarrel between Nushrok and Abazh, Yalo snatches up the fallen key. On the tower roof Gurd is set free, and there Olya for the first time holds Nushrok's terrible stare without looking away — he steps backwards, and falls. Home again through the mirror, Olya tells her grandmother that she simply looked at herself from the outside.

questions.prompt: After the quarrel, Olya's grandmother makes a wish — the one the mirror then grants. What is it?

options: That Olya could see herself from the outside
That Olya would finish one book for once
That Olya had a real friend of her own age
That Olya could live a day without a mirror

questions.explanation: The whole tale is that wish taken literally. Olya is not given a magic country for the adventure of it; she is given the chance to watch her own sulks from the outside, in a girl who behaves exactly as she does.

questions.prompt: What does a crooked mirror show the starving boy Gurd?

options: A fat boy holding an enormous loaf
An empty plate and a crust of stale bread
The royal palace laid out for a feast
Himself, but many years older than he is

questions.explanation: That is what all the kingdom's mirrors are for: not to amuse anyone but to lie in whichever direction suits their owners. A hungry person must see a well-fed one — then he will not ask why he has nothing to eat.

questions.prompt: In this kingdom names are read backwards. The boy's name, Gurd, read the other way round is the Russian word for ___.
questions.explanation: The trick works for everyone: Nushrok read backwards is the word for a kite (the bird of prey), Abazh is a toad, Anidag is a viper, and Yalo is Olya. Names in this country do not hide the truth — they give it away, if you read them the other way.

questions.prompt: What is Gurd sentenced to death for?

options: Smashing one of the crooked mirrors
Stealing bread from the royal kitchen
Refusing to bow to Nushrok in the street
Helping the two pages get into the palace

questions.explanation: Not a rebellion, not a theft, not a plot — he broke a piece of glass that was lying to his face. The punishment looks monstrous only until you see what Nushrok's power rests on: if people stop believing the mirrors, he has nothing left.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the tale in the order they happen.

items: Olya quarrels with her grandmother and is left alone
Olya steps through the mirror and meets Yalo
The girls dress as pages and get into the palace
They take the key that hangs above the king's throne
Having lost it, they go to Abazh for the second key
Gurd is freed, and Nushrok falls from the tower

questions.explanation: The plot turns on two keys, and that is deliberate: the first is won by a trick and lost at once through carelessness — very like Olya — and the second has to be fetched in earnest, from the house of the most dangerous minister of all.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their place in the kingdom.

right: Chief minister, owner of every mirror workshop
Minister who owns the rice fields, fat and cunning
The chief minister's daughter, lovely and heartless
A boy worker, chained on the roof of a tower

questions.explanation: Notice who owns what: the mirrors and the rice — that is, the lies and the food. Between them, Nushrok and Abazh hold everything a person needs both to live and to understand how they are living.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement: is it what the crooked mirrors show, or how things really are?

options.label: A well-fed boy with a big loaf of bread
A kingdom where everyone lives well
Workers with nothing at all to eat
Workshops where people bend over glass all day
Two ministers who own almost everything

questions.explanation: Every line on the left has its answer on the right: it is the same kingdom, seen in a mirror and seen plainly. Gubarev is not really writing about magic — he is writing about lying turned into a system of government.

questions.prompt: On the tower roof Nushrok steps backwards and falls. What makes the man the whole kingdom is afraid of retreat?

options: Olya looks him in the eye and does not look away
Gurd rushes at him and pushes him off the edge
Abazh betrays him and knocks the key from his hand
The king's guards surround him on the top platform

questions.explanation: Nobody pushes him. All of Nushrok's power was in a stare that made people drop their eyes, and it ends the second a girl stops dropping hers. Olya, who was a coward at the start of the book, wins simply by not turning away.

questions.prompt: Olya's grandmother wanted her to see herself from the outside. Do you think meeting Yalo actually helped Olya become better — and what exactly did she see in her? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names specific traits Olya recognises in Yalo — laziness, sulking, making excuses, fear — and says whether Olya has changed by the end. Both a confident 'yes, it helped' and a careful 'it is hard to say' earn full marks if they rest on what the girls actually do.

questions.prompt: The crooked mirrors show people not what is there but whatever suits their owners. Invent a crooked mirror for our own world: where would it hang, what untrue thing would it show and to whom — and who would benefit from that?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer covers all three parts: where the mirror is, exactly what lie it tells, and who profits. The last part matters most — it shows the child has understood what Nushrok actually uses the mirrors for.

questions.prompt: Gurd is chained on the roof and kept there until his execution. The place is called the Tower of ___.
questions.explanation: The name is not a metaphor in this book: the condemned are thrown from the top. It is from that same tower that Nushrok himself falls at the end — the man who had been using it all along.

questions.prompt: Back at home through the mirror, what does Olya tell her grandmother when asked where she has been?

options: That she simply looked at herself from the outside
That she was rescuing a boy in a faraway country
That she was visiting a friend round the corner
That she fell asleep in the hall and had a dream

questions.explanation: She answers in her grandmother's own words, which is how she says the lesson has landed without explaining anything. Then she waves to Yalo in the glass: the reflection stays where reflections belong, but Olya now knows who is looking back.
